text: Scope isolates access as well as naming. By default, a Script Include or table that lives inside one scoped application is not reachable from code running in a different scope — not Global, and not another custom application. ServiceNow assumes isolation unless a developer explicitly opens a door, rather than assuming openness unless someone explicitly locks one.

That default matters for security review and predictability — nobody auditing an application has to go hunting for hidden access paths that were never intentionally granted. There are two real, distinct mechanisms for opening that door when a legitimate cross-scope need actually exists, and they are not interchangeable.

The first is a Script Include's Accessible From field. The default, This Application Scope Only, means only code already running inside the same scope can instantiate and call it. Flipping it to All Application Scopes is a broad grant — it opens that one Script Include's entire API to every scope on the instance, with no record of which scope actually uses it or why. That's why this course treats it as the mechanism of last resort.

The second, preferred mechanism is a Cross-Scope Access Control record, stored in the sys_scope_privilege table. Each record grants one specific calling scope permission to reach one specific target — a specific Script Include, table, or API — in another scope, nothing broader. A scope granted access to one Script Include still can't reach any other Script Include or table in that application.

This is the mechanism ServiceNow recommends over broadly opening a Script Include to all scopes, specifically because it's auditable and least-privilege. Anyone reviewing the instance can see exactly which scope was granted access to exactly what, and why that grant exists, instead of discovering something was quietly opened to the entire instance.

A practical way to decide between the two: ask whether the API is genuinely generic utility code with nothing sensitive in it — a date formatter, a string sanitizer — or whether it's specific enough that you'd want a record of exactly who's allowed to call it. Generic utilities can reasonably use All Application Scopes. Anything touching real business data or security-relevant logic should get a targeted Cross-Scope Access Control grant instead.
